title: A seat at the table
subtitle: Home · Friday, 6:12 PM
focus: Words carry more than their literal meaning.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: By the time we reach my front door, Jules and I have spent forty minutes talking about our class project. We are supposed to make something about a place where we feel we belong.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I invited Jules over to work on it. Now I can hear the kitchen fan through the door, and I remember that I have not actually told Mom we are coming.

lines.speaker: Mom
lines.text: An về rồi hả? Ăn cơm chưa con?
lines.translation: You're home, An? Have you eaten yet?

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: She has a dish towel over one shoulder and a spoon in her hand. Before I answer, she is already looking behind me for another person to feed.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: What did she say? I caught your name. And I think I have heard you say cơm before.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: There is an easy answer. There is a longer answer. Mom is waiting, and Jules is still standing in the doorway with their backpack on.

note.title: A question, and a relationship
note.text: Cơm can refer to cooked rice or a meal. Here, this mother's question is both about dinner and an opening for care. That reading comes from this scene and their relationship; it is not a rule for every Vietnamese speaker or every use of the phrase.

choices.label: “Have you eaten rice yet?”
choices.reflection: You kept the image of rice. Jules needed another moment to understand the invitation.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Rice specifically? I had a sandwich. Does that count?

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I laugh, then realize it is a completely fair question. “Yes. Here she means dinner. Cơm is rice, but it can also mean a meal.”

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Bạn con ăn cùng cho vui.
reaction.translation: Your friend should eat with us. It'll be nice to have company.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “And now she is inviting you to stay.” The explanation took a detour, but Jules takes off their backpack.

choices.label: “She’s asking if I’ve eaten.”
choices.reflection: You made the practical question clear. The invitation became clear through what Mom did next.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Oh! Tell her I can go if you need to have dinner. We can work tomorrow.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “You don't have to go.” I look at Mom, who has already opened the cupboard with the bowls. “I think she is counting you in.”

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Hai đứa rửa tay đi.
reaction.translation: You two, go wash your hands.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: Jules smiles. The translation was enough to understand the question. The second bowl explains the rest.

choices.label: “She’s asking about dinner. It’s also how she checks on me.”
choices.detail: Share what the question means between you.
choices.reflection: You shared the relationship behind the question, while Mom reminded you that dinner was also quite literal.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Like my dad asking if I got home okay, even when he can see my location?

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “A little. But she also really wants to know if I've eaten.” Mom taps the spoon against the pot while I finish explaining.

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Nói gì mà lâu vậy? Cơm nguội bây giờ.
reaction.translation: What are you talking about for so long? The food is going to get cold.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: We both laugh. Explaining the feeling took longer than answering the actual question.

scenes.title: What should I call her?

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: At the sink, Jules whispers a question while Mom moves the bowls to the table. The kitchen is small enough that whispering feels more conspicuous than speaking.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: Should I call her Mrs. Nguyễn? Your mom? I don't want to be rude.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I usually call her Mẹ. Jules has heard that word, but borrowing my word for my mother would not automatically make it the right word for them.

lines.speaker: Mom
lines.text: Cứ gọi cô là cô Mai nhé.
lines.translation: You can call me cô Mai.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Mom has answered for herself. Now I have to decide how much of that answer to carry across. Jules looks from her to me, trying to follow.

scenes.prompt: How do you introduce the name Mom offered?

note.title: Let the person tell you
note.text: Vietnamese forms of address can express age and relationships as well as reference a person. Cô has several uses, including aunt-like address and teacher. In this scene, Mai states her own preference. Asking a person is more reliable than treating one English label as a universal equivalent.

choices.label: “She says you can call her Auntie Mai.”
choices.reflection: “Auntie” made the warmth accessible, but suggested a family connection Jules had to check.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: “Auntie Mai. Okay.” They pause. “Even though we're not related?”

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Yes, in this case. It is a friendly way to address her, not a claim that we are cousins.” Jules repeats the name, and Mom answers with a smile.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: The English word gave Jules a place to start. It also carried an assumption I had not meant to add.

choices.label: “Cô Mai. Cô is the way she’d like you to address her.”
choices.detail: Keep her chosen term and explain its use.
choices.reflection: You preserved Mom's chosen address. Jules needed time to try a new sound.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: “Cô Mai?” They try it quietly once, then say it to her. “Thank you for having me.”

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Không có gì. Ngồi xuống đi con.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: Mom gestures toward a chair. Jules does not suddenly know every way to use cô, but they know how she wants to be addressed tonight.

choices.label: Ask Mom whether “Mai” is okay in English.
choices.detail: Check the preference instead of deciding for her.
choices.reflection: You gave Mom a say in the translation. The conversation briefly paused to make that room.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Mẹ ơi, bạn gọi mẹ là Mai bằng tiếng Anh được không?”
reaction.translation: Mom, is it okay if my friend calls you Mai in English?

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Cô Mai nghe thân hơn. Nhưng từ từ cũng được.
reaction.translation: Cô Mai sounds warmer to me. But there's no rush.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I pass that on. Jules tries cô Mai. It took an extra exchange, but this time I did not have to guess what Mom preferred.

scenes.title: A second helping

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Dinner loosens the conversation. Jules tells a story about our classroom projector. Mom catches the word projector and tells us about a broken one at work.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I translate the parts they ask for. Other parts get across through a hand gesture, an imitation of the screen going dark, and all three of us laughing.

lines.speaker: Mom
lines.translation: Would you like a little more?

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: It was really good, but I'm full. Can you tell her? I don't want her to think I didn't like it.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Mom holds the serving spoon above Jules's bowl. I know she likes feeding people. I also know Jules gets to decide when they have had enough.

scenes.prompt: How do you pass along Jules’s answer?

note.title: Care does not cancel a boundary
note.text: The options preserve Jules's refusal. Framing can convey gratitude, but an interpreter should not replace someone's stated preference with a cultural assumption. This scene gives both the guest and the host room to say what they mean.

choices.label: “Bạn no rồi mẹ.”
choices.reflection: You preserved Jules's boundary in a few words. They chose to add their own thanks.

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Ừ, vậy thôi. Có nước trên bàn nhé.
reaction.translation: Okay, that's enough then. There's water on the table.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: “Thank you. Really, it was delicious.” They put a hand over their heart. Mom nods and sets the spoon down.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I did not need to manage every part of the exchange. They found a way to finish it together.

choices.label: “Bạn khen ngon lắm, nhưng bạn no rồi.”
choices.reflection: You carried both the compliment and the refusal, without changing either.

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Ngon là được rồi. Không cần cố ăn đâu.
reaction.translation: I'm glad it was good. No need to force yourself to eat.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I translate, and Jules lets their shoulders drop. “Thanks. I never know how much explaining is too much.”

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: Neither do I, always. Tonight the extra sentence seems to help. We carry the empty bowls to the sink.

choices.label: Help Jules say “Cảm ơn cô, con no rồi.”
choices.reflection: You invited Jules into the exchange. Practicing took time, and the refusal still remained theirs.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Only if you want to try,” I add. Jules nods, and I say the phrase slowly. They repeat it with a small pause in the middle.

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Ừ, cô hiểu rồi.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: There is no applause for the new phrase. Mom just listens and puts the spoon away. Somehow that ordinary response is the nicest part.
